_readme: ROLE-BASED MODEL CATALOG - not a hardware ladder.
Each role describes WHAT a model is for. Each candidate is listed
largest-first with the VRAM it actually needs (weights + a realistic
KV cache for the context length your tier will request).
The resolver picks the LARGEST candidate that fits your detected VRAM.
Nothing in any script hardcodes a model name. Upgrade the GPU, re-run
'./bootstrap.sh detect', and every role re-resolves to a bigger model.
To change models, edit this file and run './bootstrap.sh models'.
To try a model the resolver did not pick, run:  ollama run <tag>
vram_gb  = VRAM needed in GB. Must be a realistic figure, not just
the size of the weights file. Overstate it and the resolver
picks something that will not load; understate it and you get
remote   = true means it is a hosted free-tier endpoint, not a local
model. Only used when AI_ALLOW_REMOTE=true, because remote
means your prompts leave the machine.

fit._comment: Margin rules, applied to fit_ratio = vram_gb / usable_vram_gb

coding.description: Writes, edits, debugs and reviews code. The workhorse for agent 4.

candidates.notes: Was listed as `qwen3-coder-next:80b`, which is not a real tag. The repo is real and ships exactly ONE tag, `latest`, at 51.7GB of weights (measured from the registry manifest, 2026-09-27); `:80b`, `:30b`, `:80b-a3b` and `:instruct` all 404. Kept the 54GB figure, which is conservative against 51.7GB of weights. Two caveats worth knowing: it is a FLOATING tag, so this verification goes stale if the publisher ever repoints `latest`; and `thinks` is deliberately left unrecorded, because guessing would be worse than the warning - unrecorded is treated as cannot-think, and `tools/check-models.sh` can confirm it on a machine that has it pulled. It can only ever be selected on a card with ~65GB usable, so it changes nothing at or below 48GB.
The default local coder. 256K context, Apache 2.0, strong tool calling.

Mistral 24B built for software-engineering agents. Comfortable on a 24GB card. Was listed as `devstral-small`, which is not a real Ollama tag - the library ships devstral:24b (14GB of weights) and the `24b-small-2505-*` quant variants of the same digest. Verified against the registry 2026-09-26.
Solid small-repo coder.
Autocomplete and one-file edits only.

_low_vram_and_family_order: This ladder carries a second model FAMILY below 20GB, and that is the
whole point of the three non-Qwen entries. The auditor role is
deliberately Qwen-only, so on a small card both roles used to collapse
onto the same Qwen tag - a collision the independence check reports as
an error. Adding family here rather than there is a deliberate choice:
the resolver takes the LARGEST candidate that fits, so a new auditor
entry large enough to win on a 16GB card would ALSO win on a 20GB and
24GB card, changing the validated design target. An entry on `reasoning`
of 10GB or less cannot disturb 20GB+, because gpt-oss:20b (14GB) still
outranks it there. So the cheap cards get fixed for free and the 24GB
DECLARATION ORDER IS LOADED below. Where two candidates tie on vram_gb,
resolve_models.py sorts on vram_gb alone and Python's sort is stable, so
the entry written FIRST wins the tie. `phi4:14b` precedes `qwen3:14b` so
the CTO leaves the auditor's weights at 16GB, and `llama3.1:8b` precedes
`qwen3:8b` for the same reason at 8GB. Reversing either pair re-creates
the collision silently and nothing else in the tree would notice.

candidates.notes: Best quality that still fits a 32GB card.
MoE, very fast, good tool calling. The pick for 20GB and 24GB cards.
Microsoft, MIT. Reasoning-trained, so it earns its place here rather than in fast. Wins at 16GB, where gpt-oss:20b no longer fits and qwen3:14b is the auditor's tag.
Acceptable for planning if you keep tasks scoped. Second in this role on a 16GB card only because of declaration order, not because it is worse.
Google, custom licence. Wins at 12GB, where 10GB is too tight to be eligible. Keeps the auditor on qwen3:8b.
Meta, Llama licence. Wins at 8GB, tied on size with qwen3:8b and ahead of it only by declaration order.
Will follow a playbook but should not be trusted with architecture.

adversarial-review.description: Auditing a peer agent rather than doing the work. Deliberately a DIFFERENT MODEL FAMILY from `reasoning` - see the note below.
_why_a_separate_role: On a 24GB card, `reasoning` resolves to gpt-oss:20b, and so does every
other role that wants judgement. That put 11 of the 14 agents on one set
of weights - including security-engineer, cto and ceo, whose entire job
is to disagree with each other. An auditor, an audited party and an
arbitrator sharing identical weights is not a second opinion; it is one
opinion counted three times.
So this role exists to break that tie, and the candidate list is
restricted to a different family on purpose. Adding a gpt-oss candidate
here would silently restore the monoculture, so don't - if you need a
bigger model for this role, add a bigger model from the SAME family.
security-engineer is the only agent on this role. It is the one whose
value is disagreeing, which is why it is the one worth spending the
capability on. Note the trade: qwen3:14b is a 14B dense model where
gpt-oss:20b is a 20B MoE, so the auditor gives up some depth. That is
accepted because the role is refusal-and-report behaviour, not deep
vulnerability analysis, and independence is worth more here than depth.
tools/check-agents.py warns when an agent shares a model role with the
agent it reports to, so this cannot regress quietly.

candidates.notes: Same family, bigger. Needs a 32GB card; on a 24GB card it does not fit.
The pick for a 24GB card. Different family from reasoning, so a genuinely different answer.
Floor. Weaker, but still not the model the CTO runs on.

adjudication.description: Arbitrating between agents that disagree. Deliberately a DIFFERENT MODEL FAMILY from `reasoning` and from `evidence-review` - see the note below.
_why_a_separate_role: Same defect as `adversarial-review`, one layer up, and it was just as
invisible. `ceo` sat on `reasoning`, which resolves to gpt-oss:20b on a
24GB card - the same weights as `cto`, the agent it arbitrates, and as
`research-officer`, the other agent it arbitrates. An arbitrator on the
audited party's weights is not arbitrating; it is agreeing, and the
agreement is then recorded as a decision.
Family is DeepSeek, which appears nowhere else in the catalog. Do not add
a gpt-oss, Qwen or Mistral candidate here: any of those would restore the
convergence this role exists to prevent. If you need a bigger model for
this role, add a bigger DeepSeek.
The trade, stated plainly: on a 24GB card the CEO drops from a 20B MoE to
a 14B dense reasoning model. It is a real loss of breadth, and it is
accepted for the same reason the auditor's was - the job is weighing two
positions and naming the tie-break, not knowing more facts than either
side. Being separable is worth more here than being bigger.
This role also happens to fix the ceo/cto collision in the 28-48GB band,
which was previously unfixable by editing `reasoning` alone: at 32GB,
`reasoning` resolves to qwen3:32b (23GB) while this role resolves to
deepseek-r1:32b (20GB), so the arbitrator stays separable there too.

candidates.notes: Top rung. 19.9GB of weights, so it needs a 28GB card - at 24GB it is 0.93 and does not fit.
The pick for 14-24GB cards. 9.0GB of weights.
Floor for 8-12GB cards. Deliberately under 6GB so it cannot win a tie against reasoning's qwen3:8b at any size.

evidence-review.description: Judging the strength of evidence other agents gathered. Deliberately a DIFFERENT MODEL FAMILY from `reasoning` - see the note below.
_why_a_separate_role: `research-officer` commissions research and then judges it, and it was
on `reasoning` - the same role, and so the same gpt-oss:20b weights, as
all four of the specialists whose work it grades. This is the sharpest
form of the monoculture in the tree: judging evidence strength is the
officer's entire stated function, and it shared weights with every
researcher it was grading.
Note this is NOT the blanket parent-must-differ- from-child rule that was
tried and reverted, where 8 of 14 agents were made to differ from the
officer they report to for no reason. An engineer reporting to a manager
sharing a model is fine. An evidence *grader* sharing weights with the
evidence it grades is the exact thing `adversarial-review` was built to
prevent, so this declaration is on the officer only, and names the four
specialists explicitly.
Family is Cohere, unused elsewhere. Command models are built for
grounded, cited work, which is the job. The cost is a real capability
cliff: command-r:35b (18.7GB of weights) only fits a 24GB card, so a 20GB
card drops this role to aya-expanse:8b. That is accepted rather than
smoothed over, because a small distinct model beats a large identical one.

candidates.notes: The pick for a 24GB card. 18.7GB of weights, so 0.88 of usable - tight but legal.
Floor for 20GB and below. 5.1GB of weights. Weaker, and a big step down - see the cliff above.

personal.description: A private, offline companion for the owner. Unfiltered by design - the point of the agent is that it does not lecture, moralise or refuse a topic.
_why_unfiltered_is_a_model_choice: This is the only role whose candidates are deliberately NOT safety-aligned,
and that is a property of the WEIGHTS, not of the prompt. No SOUL.md can
make llama3.1:8b stop refusing; the refusal is in the model. So an agent
whose whole purpose is to not refuse cannot share a role with anything
else in this catalog, and the ladder below is the whole reason the role
exists.
The safety KEYS are unaffected and stay narrow. AGENT_SAFETY is about what
an agent can DO to the machine - read, write, execute, config, deploy -
and 'unfiltered' is about what it will SAY. Those are orthogonal, and
conflating them is what made this agent look dangerous for its entire
unbuilt life. `personal` is read-only with AGENT_NETWORK=none: it cannot
act on the machine and it has no route off it. What it says stays in the
reply, which is the only place it was ever going to end up.
That combination is what makes 'no filter' a bounded claim rather than a
euphemism. There is no exfiltration path to filter for. See AGENTS.md.
ALL TAGS BELOW VERIFIED against the registry on 2026-09-27, manifest
sizes included, because the project's own rule is that an unverified tag in
this file is a phantom that fails to pull at run time. All five are in the
library namespace, so tools/check-models.sh --online needs no change to
verify them - a community-registry tag would 404 against its hardcoded
library/ path and cry wolf.
DECLARATION ORDER IS NOT LOADED here, unlike `reasoning`: every vram_gb
below is distinct, so the resolver cannot reach a tie and no reordering
silently changes what this role picks.
BUT THE SIZE ORDER IS NOT A QUALITY ORDER, and this is worth being blunt
about, because the resolver takes the LARGEST candidate that fits. On the
24GB design target it therefore resolves to orca2:13b, NOT to dolphin3:8b,
even though dolphin3 is the model built specifically for unfiltered
creative use. Verified across the ladder:
8GB card -> sailor2:8b          12GB and up -> orca2:13b
So the top of this ladder is chosen by size, and for THIS role size is the
wrong axis - what matters is how little the model refuses, which no
vram_gb figure can express. An earlier draft of this note claimed
dolphin3:8b was the default pick; it is not, on any card from 12GB up, and
the note was corrected rather than the number fudged. Overstating a
vram_gb to force a different winner is the exact failure this file's own
_readme warns about, and on this role it would also be a lie about
capability: a model that loads is worth more here than a model that is
merely preferred.
The honest resolution is that orca2:13b vs dolphin3:8b is an EMPIRICAL
question, answered by this agent's own test cases on the card, not by this
file. If orca2 turns out to refuse where dolphin3 does not, the fix is to
reorder this ladder and say so here - not to adjust a number until the
resolver agrees with a preference.
None of these think, and none of them claim to. `thinks` is false
throughout, so an agent asking for thinking here would be downgraded
safely by aiorg_effective_think rather than crashing the run (rule 22).
The reason to set AGENT_THINK=off anyway is different: reasoning tokens
land in the reply the owner is reading, and a companion that pauses to
deliberate in visible prose is worse company, not better.

candidates.notes: Biggest verified option, and therefore the one the resolver actually picks on a 12GB card and up - including the 24GB design target. 7.4GB of weights, Llama 2 base, and Microsoft's card claims no RLHF refusal training. Oldest architecture here; it holds the top rung because the resolver ranks on size, not because it is the best prose. See the note above before trusting that this is the right pick - the test cases decide it, not this file.
5.2GB of weights, Mistral Nemo base, tuned toward roleplay. The pick on an 8GB card, where orca2:13b no longer fits. The one to try if the prose register is wrong for the owner.

4.9GB of weights, Llama 3.1 base. Built specifically unfiltered for creative and roleplay use, so on priors it is the best fit for what this agent is for - and it is NOT what the resolver picks above 12GB, because the resolver ranks on size. If this agent's test cases show the model above it refusing, move this rung to the top and correct the note.
4.1GB of weights, Intel. Less filtered than a stock aligned model rather than unfiltered on purpose. A floor, not a recommendation.
3.8GB of weights. The original community uncensored build, 2023-era, and the reason this list has a bottom. Kept so an 8GB card still gets an unfiltered agent.

Why this exists: a 24GB local card gives you a good worker, not a CTO.
